summary:
Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023 provides the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality", lengthy prison terms for the promotion of homosexuality, and penalties reaching 20 years for other offences under the Act. In April 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the Act's core provisions, including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years, and dismissed challenges arguing that public participation requirements had not been met. The same court had earlier voided a comparable 2013 statute on procedural grounds, leaving the 2023 Act fully in force.

Aggravated homosexuality includes sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18 and is punishable by death. Purporting to contract a same-sex marriage, or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony, carries ten years' imprisonment. A clause in the 2023 bill that would have criminalised merely identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years in prison was proposed and excluded from the enacted text. Marriage between persons of the same sex has been constitutionally prohibited since 29 September 2005, when President Museveni signed an amendment stating that such marriages are prohibited.

Enforcement has produced arrests, raids on shelters, evictions and public outings of people perceived to be LGBT, with many living in hiding; a pressure group reported in June 2024 that rights violations against the community were escalating. In February 2026 police in Arua detained two women after neighbours reported them for allegedly kissing in public, among the first known arrests under the 2023 Act.

Violence against transgender people is documented. In January 2024 a transgender woman in Kampala was mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false allegation circulated on TikTok, and sheltered with 20 others at a safe house in the city. Attacks and harassment are frequently carried out or incited by state officials, and discrimination is actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders.

In June 2021 a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala resulted in 44 arrests, with police claiming an illegal same-sex wedding was being held; several detainees alleged that police performed invasive anal examinations.

Digital exposure is a documented enforcement route. Access Now reported in May 2025 that the anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online, with digital entrapment among the main tactics authorities use through apps, and that the companies behind popular apps do too little. Amnesty International reported in October 2024 that criminalisation had shrunk online civic space, with widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation, and a climate of impunity that forces people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

Legal gender recognition is documented in a single case: in October 2021 a transgender woman, Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro, was issued identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised.
tangentialFactors:
The 2011 US State Department human rights report for Uganda listed violence and discrimination against marginalized groups, including the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community, among the three most important human rights problems in the country, during the period of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.

International condemnation of the 2023 Act has not shifted political support for comparable laws in parts of Africa.

Public opinion is hostile. A 2013 Pew survey found 96 percent of Ugandans believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, while a 2017 ILGA poll found 59 percent agreed that gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people.
localsOnly:
A person convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in childcare facilities in Uganda even after release. Minors convicted of homosexuality face three years' imprisonment.

In June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest.

In October 2010 the tabloid Rolling Stone published the names, addresses, photographs and hangouts of 100 allegedly gay and lesbian Ugandans with a call for their execution; activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper.

A 2018 article in African Health Sciences stated that Uganda's high HIV rate has roots in stigma against same-sex sexual behaviour and sex work. Human Rights Watch reported in 2005 that Uganda's abstinence-until-marriage programmes discriminated on the basis of sexual orientation, denying young LGBTQ people information that could save their lives and reinforcing stigma.

Human Rights Watch reported in May 2025 that a small group of Ugandan mothers were speaking publicly for their LGBT children.
outOfScopeNotes:
The US State Department travel advisory page for Uganda was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403). The advisory is reported to carry LGBT-specific warnings under a "Do Not Travel" rating, but its text could not be verified.

Sourced material does not describe Uganda's legal gender recognition procedure beyond the single 2021 case, and does not establish whether any process is available to visitors.

Sourced material does not address healthcare access barriers specific to transgender people.

The 2011 human rights report predates the 2023 Act and describes an earlier period.
